newsitem.title: THAILAND: IMF's Camdessus sees Thai exports pickup in 1997.
newsitem.headline: IMF's Camdessus sees Thai exports pickup in 1997.

text.p: IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus said on Tuesday that there should be improvement next year in extremely sluggish Thai export growth as the new government implemented fresh policies.

He told reporters after meeting Amnuay Viravan, the new finance minister and deputy premier, that a slowdown in Thai exports was caused by an economic sluggishness in the country's key export markets and a temporary local structural problem.
Latest central bank data last month showed that Thai exports in the first nine months of this year grew only 0.9 percent, compared to more than 20 percent in the same period last year.
"We believe that you are in a state of transition. We believe also that the exports will pick up momentum and next year should be distinctly better than what you had in 1996," he said.

Camdessus said Thailand's wide current account deficit was a cause of concern but he was confident after discussions with Amnuay that some planned new government measures would bring it under control.
Thailand's current account deficit was 8.1 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1995 and is expected by the central bank to widen further up to 8.3 percent of gdp.
He said he had been told that the government planned to use more fiscal rather than monetary measures alone as well as rebalancing of savings and investments to keep the deficit under control.
"From what I heard from your minister, the direction that the Thai government is going to take to deal with the problem is the right course," he added without giving details.
Amnuay represents the new Thai government led by premier Chavalit Yongchaiyudh which took power earlier this month.
The new government has pledged to boost the Thai economy, projected by private analysts to grow by just more than six percent after a decade of nearly nine percent growth until 1995.
Other woes it has vowed to tackle are sluggish exports growth and a widening current account deficit.
